items.title: Federated Dataset Simulation: Inducing Label-Free Heterogeneity Across Tasks
items.summary: Federated Learning enables collaborative model training across decentralized clients without sharing raw data. While the field has seen rapid growth, the datasets underpinning FL evaluation have not kept pace: real federated datasets remain scarce, and most studies rely on small-scale centralized classification datasets partitioned via Dirichlet label skew, a one-dimensional proxy for the multi-dimensional heterogeneity present in real federations. Moreover, label-based partitioning is by construction inapplicable to non-classification tasks such as segmentation and detection, for which no principled simulation method exists. We cast the conversion of centralized datasets into federated benchmarks as the task of Federated Dataset Simulation (FDS), and decompose it into a representation function $Φ$ and an assignment mechanism $π$. We provide two label-free instantiations -- geometric partitioning via pretrained model embeddings and semantic partitioning via vision-language model-derived criteria -- applicable to classification and dense prediction tasks alike. We evaluate across four datasets spanning classification, segmentation, and detection, and show that both methods induce heterogeneity that matches or exceeds that of label-skew partitioning, with measurable impact on downstream FL performance. We release fds, a modular open-source package for end-to-end federated dataset simulation, heterogeneity measurement, and FL training, at https://github.com/siomvas/fds.

items.title: DiffWAM: Learning World Action Model from Consecutive Visual Difference
items.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as an important paradigm in robot learning, jointly predicting future scene states and robot actions from current observations and instructions. However, future states entangle task-related changes with large amounts of task-irrelevant content, such as static backgrounds, which weakens the model's ability to capture changes relevant to task execution. To address this, we propose Difference World Action Model (DiffWAM), a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that enhances world representations by jointly learning future-state prediction and consecutive visual difference prediction. We define consecutive visual differences as differences between the latent representations of consecutive observations, providing an explicit learning signal for temporal variation. The framework comprises a World Expert for future frame prediction, an Action Expert for action generation, and a Diff Expert for predicting these latent differences along the trajectory. A structured unidirectional attention mask conditions the Diff, World, and Action Experts solely on the current-frame representation while blocking attention between experts. This design allows both the World and Diff Experts to be removed during inference, introducing no additional inference overhead. DiffWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks and substantially improves over FastWAM on real-world manipulation tasks. Specifically, it attains average success rates of 98.8%, 92.65%, and 88.3%, outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline (i.e., FastWAM) by 1.75, 1.55, and 15.0 percentage points, respectively.

items.title: IA-MoE: An Intensity-Aware Mixture of Experts for DNN Inference
items.summary: With the ever-increasing parameter scale and structural complexity of deep neural network (DNN) models, traditional cloud-based inference encounters bottlenecks in performance, privacy protection, and energy efficiency. While edge computing and edge intelligence facilitate the migration of inference tasks to edge servers closer to the data source, existing end-edge-cloud collaborative inference still encounters critical challenges, such as sensitivity to heterogeneous resources, complexity in multi-objective optimization, and adaptability to dynamic workloads. To achieve the joint optimization of end-to-end latency and energy consumption under dynamic inference requests with multi-resource constraints, we propose IA-MoE, an intensity-aware Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework. By modeling the model partitioning problem as a bilateral matching problem between layer tasks and virtual machine resources for each inference request, IA-MoE dynamically partitions DNN models in an edge-cloud hybrid computing environment. We evaluate IA-MoE using three representative DNNs (i.e., AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet50) on two public inference datasets in an enhanced CloudSimSDN simulation environment. Experimental results demonstrate that IA-MoE outperforms baseline methods regarding weighted normalized metrics for end-to-end latency and energy consumption. To our knowledge, this is the first study to introduce the MoE paradigm for DNN partitioning and collaborative inference in hybrid computing environments, providing a practical solution for efficient inference in artificial intelligence applications.

items.title: Trading Parameters for Accuracy in MambaVision for Chest Radiograph Classification
items.summary: MambaVision, a hybrid state-space and attention backbone, places most of its parameters in its widest, fourth stage. We quantified what that stage contributes to multi-label chest radiograph classification. The fourth stage was replaced with lighter single-scan state-space blocks adapted from Spatial-Mamba, with multi-scale dilated depthwise convolutions applied to the scan output; the first three stages were retained. Tiny, Small, and Base models were evaluated across nine dataset-scale combinations drawn from two source cohorts: the National Institutes of Health ChestX-ray14 archive (full ChestMNIST and a high-resolution subset) and Indiana University Open-i. At the Tiny scale, replacement reduced parameter count by 35.7% and increased graphics processing unit throughput by 19.3%; the savings came from the stage's dense projections, not from removing quadratic attention. Without distillation, the mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve on ChestMNIST was 0.004 lower than the baseline (95% bootstrap confidence interval, 0.002 to 0.006), and 0.003 to 0.006 lower across all nine combinations. Knowledge distillation from an unreplaced teacher narrowed the gap to the undistilled baseline to 0.001-0.002 and met the equivalence criterion on ChestMNIST, but distilling the baseline with the same recipe improved it by 0.001-0.003, so a gap of 0.002-0.005 persisted under symmetric training. At the Base scale, the unreplaced Small model was both smaller and more accurate. Fourth-stage replacement is a useful trade-off only for Tiny and Small models. These measurements let developers of chest radiograph screening tools weigh model size and speed against a quantified loss of diagnostic discrimination.

items.title: DAPPT: Domain-Aware Policies from Procedural Trajectories for Sim-to-Real Dexterous Tool Use
items.summary: Sim-to-real RL has achieved impressive results in dexterous manipulation but remains limited to tasks with accurate rigid-body simulation. However, these methods cannot be applied to skills that involve deformable and particles, with which the simulation speed will become too slow for large-scale RL learning. We present DAPPT, a sim-to-real framework for end-to-end dexterous tool-use manipulation skills, e.g., sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, without simulating non-rigid materials. Our method learns a domain-aware RL policy by tracking procedural trajectories parameterized by domain parameters, and distills it into an end-to-end domain-aware sensorimotor policy. Furthermore, explicit domain represen-tation enables fast selection of domain parameters that can maximize downstream task performance. We evaluate DAPPT end-to-end on six dexterous manipulation tasks, including sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, sand scraping, mouse-wheel scrolling, dispenser pressing, and spray triggering. Our method achieves 1.5-3.8x in task metrics through the best domain parameter and transfers zero-shot to the real world.

items.title: SliceWise: Traffic-Aware Multi-Agent RL with Temporal Encoding for Joint Slice Admission and Resource Orchestration in O-RAN
items.summary: Ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) services in mission-critical applications such as industrial automation, remote healthcare, and autonomous systems demand stringent quality-of-service (QoS) guarantees under dynamic, resource-constrained wireless conditions. Open radio access networks (O-RAN) offer a software-defined and programmable foundation for embedding AI-driven control. This letter proposes SliceWise, a traffic-aware multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MARL) framework for joint admission control, user-slice association, and resource orchestration in O-RAN. The control problem is modeled as a cooperative multi-agent Markov decision process, with long short-term memory (LSTM) networks capturing temporal traffic dynamics and dueling double deep Q-networks (D3QN) ensuring stable learning. Simulation results show that SliceWise substantially reduces delay violations and packet drops while improving slice-level reliability and resource efficiency, offering a scalable orchestration solution for AI-native O-RAN deployments.

items.title: From Sensors to Silicon: Causal Cross-Layer Self-Healing Edge AI for Secure and Energy-Adaptive IoT Systems
items.summary: The migration of artificial intelligence from centralized cloud infrastructure to resource-constrained Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices reduces communication latency and improves data locality, but it also tightly couples sensing quality, inference behavior, microarchitectural activity, hardware reliability, security, and energy management within the same physical node. Existing edge-intelligence solutions predominantly address these dimensions in isolation, making it difficult to determine whether an observed degradation originates from sensor malfunction, data-distribution shift, malicious execution, hardware faults, or resource and thermal stress. This paper presents a causal cross-layer self-healing Edge-AI framework that continuously observes synchronized telemetry spanning sensor health, inference uncertainty, processor hardware-performance counters, accelerator and memory activity, power and thermal state, and communication conditions. A temporally informed causal reasoning engine estimates the most probable origin of abnormal behavior and quantifies diagnostic uncertainty, including under concurrent perturbations.

items.title: Run, Read Back, Refine: Observation Fidelity in Execution-Grounded EDA Agents
items.summary: Design engineers lose the most time orchestrating flows and patching the gaps where closed EDA tools refuse to interoperate. We present an execution-grounded LLM agent for PyAether, SKILL, and Tcl that closes a generate-execute-refine loop over unified MCP tools (API retrieval, documentation, sandbox execution) and is already deployed in production EDA flows, with a grounding-gap framework positing that EDA-scripting correctness is bottlenecked by observation fidelity at the L4 (situated) layer, which model scale alone cannot reach. On EDA-Scripting-Bench (449 tasks, three languages, four commercial runtimes), the system reaches 76.5% pooled Pass@1 versus 19.7% (pure LLM): the system-level observation axis spans 56.8 percentage points with the model fixed, exceeding the 23.3-percentage-point backbone range with the harness fixed---two axes answering different questions; observation is an under-invested axis whose returns are measurable and graded.

items.title: Exstill: The Most Efficient Single-Chip Processor for the Next Token
items.summary: Generating a token with a language model requires a fixed amount of arithmetic, whose energy sets a floor beneath any hardware. For Qwen3-1.7B at a 16K-token context, gate-level measurements at 5 nm place this floor at 0.89 mJ per token, yet an NVIDIA B300 spends 391-1,120x that. The excess is the price of generality, software layers, programmable hardware and moving weights and key-value (KV) caches from external memory, and it widens with each process generation. We present a co-design approach that brings token generation close to this floor and then lowers the floor itself, optimizing silicon and model together in a gate-level search loop. Fixing one model architecture in the datapath, with weights still loadable, and holding weights and every conversation's KV cache on-die, a pre-silicon 5 nm design brings an unchanged Qwen3-1.7B token to 3.4x its floor. Co-designing the model with the circuits at fixed quality lowers the floor to 0.29 mJ and the token to 0.52 mJ, 1.8x the new floor and less than the baseline model's arithmetic alone, while on-die capacity grows from one user to twelve. Against a measured B300 serving the same twelve users, the design decodes each user's tokens 110x faster at 690x lower energy. To show that one fixed architecture can serve, as a co-processor, the latency-critical workloads around a frontier model, we introduce Polyglot-DC (1.7B and 4B, each with its own design), specialized for each job by distillation and task-specific training into its own weights. As a drafter it speeds single-user speculative decoding of large open models by up to 6.6x at the maximum reasoning effort. Its guard returns multilingual verdicts in a millisecond or less, within a point of the strongest open guard. Its agent and financial-reasoning models lead comparable open models on established benchmarks, with a reasoning turn falling from seconds to tens of milliseconds.

items.title: PRISM: A Post-Prediction Reliability Framework for Evidence-Guided Correction and Selective Abstention
items.summary: A model may produce a prediction with high confidence and still get the outcome wrong. This is a challenge in sequential applications, where the system evolves over time and deployment data may differ from the data used during training. To address this issue, we propose PRISM (Prediction Reliability and Intelligent Self-Correction Mechanism), a framework that evaluates prediction reliability after the initial output is generated. It estimates the risk of error and examines predictions identified as potentially unreliable. For these cases, PRISM analyses available signals, retrieves similar situations from historical data, and verifies whether an alternative prediction is supported by the evidence. It can then retain the original prediction, apply a verified correction, or abstain when the evidence is insufficient. We evaluate PRISM on second-innings match prediction in the Indian Premier League (IPL). Ball-by-ball records are converted into over-level observations to capture changes in match conditions throughout an innings. To preserve temporal order, earlier IPL seasons are used for training, IPL 2024 for validation, and IPL 2025-2026 for out-of-time testing. The dataset contains 8,665 over-level observations from 475 matches, with the test partition comprising 2,568 observations from 142 matches. In one experimental record, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and HistGradientBoosting achieve accuracies of 65.2%, 68.4%, and 70.2%, respectively. The corresponding PRISM evaluation reports a selective accuracy of 82.4% at 88.5% coverage, with a Brier score of 0.126 and an expected calibration error (ECE) of 0.019.

items.title: DoF-Query Transformer for Adaptive Fusion of Egocentric Vision and Forearm HD-sEMG in Continuous Hand Kinematics
items.summary: Continuous and accurate estimation of human hand kinematics is important not only for intuitive human-machine interaction, but also for capturing fine-grained human manipulation demonstrations that can provide action supervision for embodied-intelligence datasets and dexterous robot learning. However, individual sensing modalities may be insufficient for reliable estimation under varying operating conditions. We present a finger-unencumbered multimodal framework for continuous regression of 20 hand joint angles from egocentric RGB images and 128-channel forearm high-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG). The framework combines a Vision Transformer-based visual encoder, a Transformer-based EMG encoder, and a degree of freedom (DoF) query Transformer fusion decoder. To account for the varying informativeness of visual and EMG cues across joint DoFs and input conditions, the decoder assigns a separate learnable query to each DoF, enabling DoF-specific and context-adaptive fusion of the two modalities. The framework was evaluated on synchronized multimodal data from 10 participants. Averaged across participants, the proposed fusion model achieved a mean coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of $0.88$ and a mean absolute error (MAE) of $2.80^\circ$, compared with $0.82$ and $3.21^\circ$ for the vision-only model and $0.68$ and $5.13^\circ$ for the EMG-only model. It also outperformed the evaluated representative unimodal baselines and alternative fusion designs. DoF-wise analyses showed larger fusion gains for visually ambiguous joints and viewing conditions, while synthetic visual occlusion demonstrated greater robustness than vision-only estimation. These results highlight the complementary value of egocentric vision and forearm HD-sEMG for capturing fine-grained human hand kinematics, with potential applications in human demonstration acquisition and dexterous robot learning.

items.title: ReactBench-AD: Do Driving VLAs and World-Action Models React to Imminent Hazards in Their Path?
items.summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce ReactBench-AD, a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain. Code and data will be made publicly available.

items.title: Gradient-based Planning for World Models at Longer Horizons
items.summary:
GRASP is a new gradient-based planner for learned dynamics (a "world model") that makes long-horizon planning practical by (1) lifting the trajectory into virtual states so optimization is parallel across time, (2) adding stochasticity directly to the state iterates for exploration, and (3) reshaping gradients so actions get clean signals while we avoid brittle "state-input" gradients through high-dimensional vision models. Large, learned world models are becoming increasingly capable. They can predict long sequences of future observations in high-dimensional visual spaces and generalize across tasks in ways that were difficult to imagine a few years ago. As these models scale, they start to look less like task-specific predictors and more like general-purpose simulators. But having a powerful predictive model is not the same as being able to use it effectively for control/learning/planning. In practice, long-horizon planning with modern world models remains fragile: optimization becomes ill-conditioned, non-greedy structure creates bad local minima, and high-dimensional latent spaces introduce subtle failure modes. In this blog post, I describe the problems that motivated this project and our approach to address them: why planning with modern world models can be surprisingly fragile, why long horizons are the real stress test, and what we changed to make gradient-based planning much more robust. This blog post discusses work done with Mike Rabbat, Aditi Krishnapriyan, Yann LeCun, and Amir Bar (* denotes equal advisorship), where we propose GRASP. What is a world model? These days, the term "world model" is quite overloaded, and depending on the context can either mean an explicit dynamics model or some implicit, reliable internal state that a generative model relies on (e.g. when an LLM generates chess moves, whether there is some internal representation of the board). We give our loose working definition below. Suppose you take actions $a_t \in \mathcal{A}$ and observe states $s_t \in \mathcal{S}$ (images, latent vectors, proprioception). A world model is a learned model that, given the current state and a sequence of future actions, predicts what will happen next. Formally, it defines a predictive distribution on a sequence of observed states $s_{t-h:t}$ and current action $a_t$: \[P_	heta(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t-h:t},\; a_t)\] that approximates the environment's true conditional $P(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t-h:t},\; a_t)$. For this blog post, we'll assume a Markovian model $P(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t-h:t},\; a_t)$ for simplicity (all results here can be extended to the more general case), and when the model is deterministic it reduces to a map over states: \[s_{t+1} = F_	heta(s_t, a_t).\] In practice the state $s_t$ is often a learned latent representation (e.g., encoded from pixels), so the model operates in a (theoretically) compact, differentiable space. The key point is that a world model gives you a differentiable simulator ; you can roll it forward under hypothetical action sequences and backpropagate through the predictions. Planning: choosing actions by optimizing through the model Given a start $s_0$ and a goal $g$, the simplest planner chooses an action sequence $\mathbf{a}=(a_0,\dots,a_{T-1})$ by rolling out the model and minimizing terminal error: \[\min_{\mathbf{a}} \; \| s_T(\mathbf{a}) - g \|_2^2, \quad 	ext{where } s_T(\mathbf{a}) = \mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}(s_0,\mathbf{a}).\] Here we use $\mathcal{F}^T$ as shorthand for the full rollout through the world model (dependence on model parameters $	heta$ is implicit): \[\mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}(s_0, \mathbf{a}) = F_	heta(F_	heta(\cdots F_	heta(s_0, a_0), \cdots, a_{T-2}), a_{T-1}).\] In short horizons and low-dimensional systems, this can work reasonably well. But as horizons grow and models become larger and more expressive, its weaknesses become amplified. So why doesn't this just work at scale? Why long-horizon planning is hard (even when everything is differentiable) There are two separate pain points for the more general world model, plus a third that is specific to learned, deep learning-based models. 1) Long-horizon rollouts create deep, ill-conditioned computation graphs Those familiar with backprop through time (BPTT) may notice that we're differentiating through a model applied to itself repeatedly, which will lead to the exploding/vanishing gradients problem. Namely, if we take derivatives (note we're differentiating vector-valued functions, resulting in Jacobians that we denote with $D_x (\cdots)$) with respect to earlier actions (e.g. $a_0$): \[D_{a_0} \mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}(s_0, \mathbf{a}) = \Bigl(\prod_{t=1}^T D_s F_	heta(s_t, a_t)\Bigr) D_{a_0}F_	heta(s_0, a_0).\] We see that the Jacobian's conditioning scales exponentially with time $T$: \[\sigma_{	ext{max/min}}(D_{a_0}\mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}) \sim \sigma_{	ext{max/min}}(D_s F_	heta)^{T-1},\] leading to exploding or vanishing gradients. 2) The landscape is non-greedy and full of traps At short horizons, the greedy solution, where we move straight toward the goal at every step, is often good enough. If you only need to plan a few steps ahead, the optimal trajectory usually doesn't deviate much from "head toward $g$" at each step. As horizons grow, two things happen. First, longer tasks are more likely to require non-greedy behavior: going around a wall, repositioning before pushing, backing up to take a better path. And as horizons grow, more of these non-greedy steps are typically needed. Second, the optimization space itself scales with horizon: $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{A} 	imes \cdots 	imes \mathcal{A}) = T\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{A})$, further expanding the space of local minima for the optimization problem. Distance to goal along the optimal path is non-monotonic, and the resulting loss landscape can be rough. A long-horizon fix: lifting the dynamics constraint Suppose we treat the dynamics constraint $s_{t+1} = F_{	heta}(s_t, a_t)$ as a soft constraint, and we instead optimize the following penalty function over both actions $(a_0,\ldots,a_{T-1})$ and states $(s_0,\ldots,s_T)$: \[\min_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta(s_t,a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2, \quad 	ext{with } s_0 	ext{ fixed and } s_T=g.\] This is also sometimes called collocation in planning/robotics literature. Note the lifted formulation shares the same global minimizers as the original rollout objective (both are zero exactly when the trajectory is dynamically feasible). But the optimization landscapes are very different, and we get two immediate benefits: Each world model evaluation $F_{	heta}(s_t,a_t)$ depends only on local variables, so all $T$ terms can be computed in parallel across time , resulting in a huge speed-up for longer horizons, and You no longer backpropagate through a single deep $T$-step composition to get a learning signal, since the previous product of Jacobians now splits into a sum, e.g.: \[D_{a_0} \mathcal{L} = 2(F_	heta(s_0, a_0) - s_1).\] Being able to optimize states directly also helps with exploration, as we can temporarily navigate through unphysical domains to find the optimal plan: Collocation-based planning allows us to directly perturb states and explore midpoints more effectively. However, lunch is never free. And indeed, especially for deep learning-based world models, there is a critical issue that makes the above optimization quite difficult in practice. An issue for deep learning-based world models: sensitivity of state-input gradients The tl;dr of this section is: directly optimizing states through a deep learning-based $F_{	heta}$ is incredibly brittle, à la adversarial robustness . Even if you train your world model in a lower-dimensional state space, the training process for the world model makes unseen state landscapes very sharp, whether it be an unseen state itself or simply a normal/orthogonal direction to the data manifold. Adversarial robustness and the "dimpled manifold" model Adversarial robustness originally looked at classification models $f_	heta : \mathbb{R}^{w	imes h 	imes c} 	o \mathbb{R}^K$, and showed that by following the gradient of a particular logit $
abla f_	heta^k$ from a base image $x$ (not of class $k$), you did not have to move far along $x' = x + \epsilon
abla f_	heta^k$ to make $f_	heta$ classify $x'$ as $k$ ( Szegedy et al., 2014 ; Goodfellow et al., 2015 ): Depiction of the classic example from (Goodfellow et al., 2015). Later work has painted a geometric picture for what's going on: for data near a low-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}$, the training process controls behavior in tangential directions, but does not regularize behavior in orthogonal directions, thus leading to sensitive behavior ( Stutz et al., 2019 ). Another way stated: $f_	heta$ has a reasonable Lipschitz constant when considering only tangential directions to the data manifold $\mathcal{M}$, but can have very high Lipschitz constants in normal directions. In fact, it often benefits the model to be sharper in these normal directions, so it can fit more complicated functions more precisely. As a result, such adversarial examples are incredibly common even for a single given model. Further, this is not just a computer vision phenomenon; adversarial examples also appear in LLMs ( Wallace et al., 2019 ) and in RL ( Gleave et al., 2019 ). While there are methods to train for more adversarially robust models, there is a known trade-off between model performance and adversarial robustness ( Tsipras et al., 2019 ): especially in the presence of many weakly-correlated variables, the model must be sharper to achieve higher performance. Indeed, most modern training algorithms, whether in computer vision or LLMs, do not train adversarial robustness out. Thus, at least until deep learning sees a major regime change, this is a problem we're stuck with . Why is adversarial robustness an issue for world model planning? Consider a single component of the dynamics loss we're optimizing in the lifted state approach: \[\min_{s_t, a_t, s_{t+1}} \|F_	heta(s_t, a_t) - s_{t+1}\|_2^2\] Let's further focus on just the base state: \[\min_{s_t} \|F_	heta(s_t, a_t) - s_{t+1}\|_2^2.\] Since world models are typically trained on state/action trajectories $(s_1, a_1, s_2, a_2, \ldots)$, the state-data manifold for $F_{	heta}$ has dimensionality bounded by the action space: \[\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{M}_s) \le \mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{A}) + 1 + \mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{R}),\] where $\mathcal{R}$ is some optional space of augmentations (e.g. translations/rotations). Thus, we can typically expect $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{M}_s)$ to be much lower than $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{S})$, and thus: it is very easy to find adversarial examples that hack any state to any other desired state. As a result, the dynamics optimization \[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta(s_t,a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2\] feels incredibly "sticky," as the base points $s_t$ can easily trick $F_{	heta}$ into thinking it's already made its local goal. 1 1. This adversarial robustness issue, while particularly bad for lifted-state approaches, is not unique to them. Even for serial optimization methods that optimize through the full rollout map $\mathcal{F}^T$, it is possible to get into unseen states, where it is very easy to have a normal component fed into the sensitive normal components of $D_s F_{	heta}$. The action Jacobian's chain rule expansion is \[\Bigl(\prod_{t=1}^T D_s F_	heta(s_t, a_t)\Bigr) D_{a_0}F_	heta(s_0, a_0).\] See what happens if any stage of the product has any component normal to the data manifold. ↩ Our fix This is where our new planner GRASP comes in. The main observation: while $D_s F_{	heta}$ is untrustworthy and adversarial, the action space is usually low-dimensional and exhaustively trained, so $D_a F_{	heta}$ is actually reasonable to optimize through and doesn't suffer from the adversarial robustness issue! The action input is usually lower-dimensional and densely trained (the model has seen every action direction), so action gradients are much better behaved. At its core, GRASP builds a first-order lifted state / collocation-based planner that is only dependent on action Jacobians through the world model. We thus exploit the differentiability of learned world models $F_{	heta}$, while not falling victim to the inherent sensitivity of the state Jacobians $D_s F_{	heta}$. GRASP: Gradient RelAxed S tochastic P lanner As noted before, we start with the collocation planning objective, where we lift the states and relax dynamics into a penalty: \[\min_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta(s_t,a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2, \quad 	ext{with } s_0 	ext{ fixed and } s_T=g.\] We then make two key additions. Ingredient 1: Exploration by noising the state iterates Even with a smoother objective, planning is nonconvex. We introduce exploration by injecting Gaussian noise into the virtual state updates during optimization. A simple version: \[s_t \leftarrow s_t - \eta_s 
abla_{s_t}\mathcal{L} + \sigma_{	ext{state}} \xi, \qquad \xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I).\] Actions are still updated by non-stochastic descent: \[a_t \leftarrow a_t - \eta_a 
abla_{a_t}\mathcal{L}.\] The state noise helps you "hop" between basins in the lifted space, while the actions remain guided by gradients. We found that specifically noising states here (as opposed to actions) finds a good balance of exploration and the ability to find sharper minima. 2 2. Because we only noise the states (and not the actions), the corresponding dynamics are not truly Langevin dynamics. ↩ Ingredient 2: Reshape gradients: stop brittle state-input gradients, keep action gradients As discussed, the fragile pathway is the gradient that flows into the state input of the world model, \(D_s F_{	heta}\) . The most straightforward way to do this initially is to just stop state gradients into \(F_{	heta}\) directly: Let $ ar{s}_t$ be the same value as $s_t$, but with gradients stopped. Define the stop-gradient dynamics loss : \[\mathcal{L}_{	ext{dyn}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta( ar{s}_t, a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2.\] This alone does not work. Notice now states only follow the previous state's step, without anything forcing the base states to chase the next ones. As a result, there are trivial minima for just stopping at the origin, then only for the final action trying to get to the goal in one step. Dense goal shaping We can view the above issue as the goal's signal being cut off entirely from previous states. One way to fix this is to simply add a dense goal term throughout prediction: \[\mathcal{L}_{	ext{goal}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta( ar{s}_t, a_t) - g ig\|_2^2.\] In normal settings this would over-bias towards the greedy solution of straight chasing the goal, but this is balanced in our setting by the stop-gradient dynamics loss's bias towards feasible dynamics. The final objective is then as follows: \[\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) = \mathcal{L}_{	ext{dyn}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) + \gamma \, \mathcal{L}_{	ext{goal}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}).\] The result is a planning optimization objective that does not have dependence on state gradients. Periodic "sync": briefly return to true rollout gradients The lifted stop-gradient objective is great for fast, guided exploration , but it's still an approximation of the original serial rollout objective. So every $K_{	ext{sync}}$ iterations, GRASP does a short refinement phase: Roll out from $s_0$ using current actions $\mathbf{a}$, and take a few small gradient steps on the original serial loss: \[\mathbf{a} \leftarrow \mathbf{a} - \eta_{	ext{sync}}\,
abla_{\mathbf{a}}\,\|s_T(\mathbf{a})-g\|_2^2.\] The lifted-state optimization still provides the core of the optimization, while this refinement step adds some assistance to keep states and actions grounded towards real trajectories. This refinement step can of course be replaced with a serial planner of your choice (e.g. CEM); the core idea is to still get some of the benefit of the full-path synchronization of serial planners, while still mostly using the benefits of the lifted-state planning. How GRASP addresses long-range planning Collocation-based planners offer a natural fix for long-horizon planning, but this optimization is quite difficult through modern world models due to adversarial robustness issues. GRASP proposes a simple solution for a smoother collocation-based planner, alongside stable stochasticity for exploration . As a result, longer-horizon planning ends up not only succeeding more, but also finding such successes faster: Push-T demo: longer-horizon planning with GRASP. Horizon CEM GD LatCo GRASP H=40 61.4% / 35.3s 51.0% / 18.0s 15.0% / 598.0s 59.0% / 8.5s H=50 30.2% / 96.2s 37.6% / 76.3s 4.2% / 1114.7s 43.4% / 15.2s H=60 7.2% / 83.1s 16.4% / 146.5s 2.0% / 231.5s 26.2% / 49.1s H=70 7.8% / 156.1s 12.0% / 103.1s 0.0% / — 16.0% / 79.9s H=80 2.8% / 132.2s 6.4% / 161.3s 0.0% / — 10.4% / 58.9s Push-T results. Success rate (%) / median time to success. Bold = best in row. Note the median success time will bias higher with higher success rate; GRASP manages to be faster despite higher success rate. What's next? There is still plenty of work to be done for modern world model planners. We want to exploit the gradient structure of learned world models, and collocation (lifted-state optimization) is a natural approach for long-horizon planning, but it's crucial to understand typical gradient structure here: smooth and informative action gradients and brittle state gradients. We view GRASP as an initial iteration for such planners. Extension to diffusion-based world models (deeper latent timesteps can be viewed as smoothed versions of the world model itself), more sophisticated optimizers and noising strategies, and integrating GRASP into either a closed-loop system or RL policy learning for adaptive long-horizon planning are all natural and interesting next steps. I do genuinely think it's an exciting time to be working on world model planners. It's a funny sweet spot where the background literature (planning and control overall) is incredibly mature and well-developed, but the current setting (pure planning optimization over modern, large-scale world models) is still heavily underexplored. But, once we figure out all the right ideas, world model planners will likely become as commonplace as RL. For more details, read the full paper or visit the project website . items.title: NEMESIS2.0: LLM-Aided Netlist-Driven Performance Equation Modeling for Accelerated Analog Circuit Sizing
items.summary: This work presents NEMESIS2.0, an open-source LLM-aided framework that automatically derives equation-based performance models for analog circuits. The resulting equations provide fast, accurate surrogates for SPICE evaluation. To validate the method, equation-based models are developed for seven circuit test cases in a commercial 65nm CMOS technology, covering 15 metrics on five operational transconductance amplifier topologies, and six metrics on two dynamic comparator topologies. When tested on 1000 unseen variants of these seven designs, each corresponding to a different set of independently sampled transistor sizes, the accuracy is found to be within 5% of SPICE. To demonstrate use cases for NEMESIS2.0, the generated models are used as performance evaluators in multiple transistor sizers based on different population-based stochastic search optimizers. For each of the seven test cases, transistor sizing is performed for 100 different sets of performance specifications, with final SPICE simulation confirming that 83.3% of the resulting designs meet all specifications after a single sizing run. The rest fail to meet the specifications due to discrepancies between the model and SPICE, and require iterative resizing under tightened specifications; all such scenarios meet specifications within five iterations. Within the transistor sizers, this equation-based performance analysis evaluates ~400 design candidates per second, versus 0.14 candidates per second for SPICE-based evaluation, achieving 196-238x sizing runtime speedup, including final SPICE verification.

items.title: EasyNav: A Modular Architecture for Real-Time Navigation Across Heterogeneous Robot Environments
items.summary: Most robot navigation stacks implicitly bind mapping, localization, planning, and control to specific representations and data flows, yielding architectures hard to extend, compare experimentally, or reason about end-to-end timing. This is critical in heterogeneous scenarios, where multiple spatial representations, sensing modalities, and coordinate frames coexist and evolve at different rates. This paper presents a navigation architecture centered on an explicit, shared navigation state that serves as the sole interaction interface between modular components. Constraining mapping, localization, planning, and control to operate over this shared state enables interchangeable, representation-agnostic pipelines under explicit compatibility and timing contracts. We realize this architecture as EasyNav, an open source ROS 2 framework, and validate it through real-robot experiments, including indoor navigation with laser sensing and large-scale indoor-outdoor navigation with GPS and 3D LiDAR across multi-level routes. Compared with Nav2 under matched conditions, EasyNav reduces reaction latency from 377 to 33 ms indoors and from 71 to 8 ms outdoors, while also using less CPU and memory.

items.title: Sustaining In-Network Computation in Satellite Networks: An Architecture for Semantic Continuity
items.summary: Satellite computations often outlast the paths and providers initially serving them. We argue that in-network computing should organize changing execution opportunities around one continuing logical computation: workers execute ready operations, while consumers recognize which results already contribute. We present an architecture separating logical computation, stream context, and physical binding, and show in wildfire assessment how retained observations support recomputation while reachable association history stays in place. A 300-node Linux prototype examines placement, dependency assembly, and continuation. Across 120 images, stage-wise placement delivers 82.08% of positions within deadlines versus 76.06% for single-node placement, while traces separate blocked output delivery from dependencies split across providers. items.title: SMELL: Sparsity-aware Memory Efficient Federated Fine-tuning for Long-context LLMs
items.summary: Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial challenges arising from excessive activation memory, heterogeneous token-importance patterns across clients, and communication overhead. To address these challenges, we propose SMELL, a Sparsity-aware and Memory-Efficient federated fine-tuning framework for Long-context LLMs. SMELL integrates three complementary mechanisms: Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR). These mechanisms jointly enable memory-efficient local adaptation, heterogeneity-aware sparsity coordination, and lightweight model-update transmission. Experiments on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B demonstrate that SMELL reduces peak memory consumption by up to 88.35% compared with conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% compared with forward-only LoRA fine-tuning at a 16K context length. Furthermore, SMELL improves fine-tuning performance under certain non-IID settings and supports compact update transmission with progressive reconstruction, demonstrating its potential for resource-efficient federated long-context LLM adaptation.

items.title: Can Agentic LLMs Write Task-Based Parallel Code? A Study of OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU and TTG
items.summary: Task-based programming offers more expressive power than loop-level parallelism, but the runtimes providing it differ widely in API style, maturity, and the amount of public code to learn from. This paper asks how well LLM agents write C++ for four of them: OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU, and TTG. Instead of single one-shot prompts, we use an agentic workflow in which the model edits files, compiles, and runs its kernels until it reproduces a reference output. Five locally hosted open-weight LLM implement seven HPC kernels, including matrix multiplication, Cholesky and LU factorization, in all four frameworks and a serial baseline to verify their understanding of the problem in general. Every kernel is evaluated independently for correctness at each concurrency level, strong scaling, and peak memory. Model capability dominates the outcome: three models produce correct, genuinely task-parallel kernels in 57-82% of the cases, while two models rarely compile their own code and almost never succeed. For the capable models, OpenMP Tasking and HPX are handled most reliably, StarPU is close behind, and TTG trails. The best generated GEMM and factorization kernels match or exceed the multithreaded OpenBLAS/LAPACK reference. However, correctness overstates parallel quality: several "parallel" kernels contain no parallelism at all; and serialized task graphs and unsuitable task granularity remain common.

items.title: Towards Agentic Scientific Discovery in Distributed Systems

items.title: Delayed Heuristic-Behavior-Target Coupling for Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning in Inventory Control
items.summary: Many reinforcement learning methods tie data collection to the task policy, while coordinating independently optimized behavior and target policies remains challenging. Policies learned by these methods can perform unreliably in long-horizon tasks under uncertainty, such as inventory control, where failures can incur extreme costs. We introduce Heuristic Behavior Policy Optimization (HBPO), an off-policy framework that routes heuristic guidance through persistent behavior learning, coupled with target-policy, updating separately with residual-based advantage estimation and emphatic weighting. Under matched environment interaction budgets on DSIS and its risk-augmented variant DSIS-RB, HBPO recovers many high-cost initial policies and improves most non-collapse comparison groups. Cold starts achieve competitive costs without final cost collapse across all tested seeds. We identify a transmission chain in the delayed heuristic-behavior-target coupling as a key driver of recovery and improvement. Generation-level diagnostics trace heuristic uptake and subsequent selective target responses, while component ablations support the contribution of this transmission mechanism to policy recovery and improvement.

items.title: PlanDiv: Test-Time Scaling with Latent Plans for Vision-Language-Action Models
items.summary: Test-time scaling improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies by drawing several action candidates and executing the best one. We find that its returns diminish quickly when the candidates are resampled from one decoder: they differ by noise rather than by plan, and for each of three resampling sources, going from four to eight candidates adds only 0.06-0.07 to the average number of completed tasks on CALVIN. We introduce PlanDiv, an action head that makes the candidates differ by plan: a lightweight planner proposes K latent plan hypotheses, a shared masked-diffusion executor decodes one action chunk per plan from a single backbone pass, and the policy executes the chunk that its own likelihood ranks highest. The plans are learned from demonstrations alone, without plan labels or rewards. With the backbone, data and training recipe held fixed, eight plan-conditioned candidates raise five-task chain success on CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D from 56.9% to 69.9%, while eight candidates from autoregressive, plan-free or same-plan resampling reach at most 64.9%. The same-plan baseline is PlanDiv's own checkpoint with the plan held fixed, so this gap comes from the plans, not from drawing more samples. On LIBERO-Long, four plans remove 40% of single-candidate failures, against at most 21% for matched resampling. On a real Franka arm the gain appears where a task admits more than one solution: PlanDiv is on par with a single-output OpenVLA-OFT+ baseline on a one-solution task and succeeds in 51 of 54 trials against 40 of 54 on two tasks with two solutions.

items.title: Rethinking KV Caching for LLM Decode: Free-Space Optical KV Regeneration for Reduction of Memory Traffic
items.summary: Long-context large language model (LLM) decoding repeatedly reads the historical key-value (KV) cache, making multi-head attention (MHA) memory-bandwidth-bound. Caching layer-input activations instead halves historical-cache storage and traffic, but requires regenerating KV from each cached activation. On digital accelerators such as GPUs, this regeneration takes far longer than fetching the activation from HBM. The KV regeneration overhead outweighs the savings from reduced memory traffic, shifting decode attention from a memory bottleneck to a compute bottleneck. We present OptiDecode, a hybrid optoelectronic decode-attention accelerator that regenerates historical KV using free-space optics and computes attention digitally. Projection weights remain resident on optical tiles, exploiting reuse across historical tokens for high-throughput optical regeneration. Scaling to large models introduces two challenges. First, distributing weights across tiles requires sending the same activations to every head group, while each readout die produces only partial KV. Activation replay shares one set of electrical-to-optical converters across head groups without costly broadcast. In-situ attention avoids transferring partial KV from readout dies to reducers by computing on them locally and exchanging only partial scores, probabilities, and partial outputs. Second, processing an activation chunk through all dependent stages takes longer than one activation-fetch interval. Chunk pipelining overlaps successive chunks so that OptiDecode sustains the HBM activation-fetch rate. OptiDecode demonstrates 1.92-1.99x decode-attention speedup over an ideal GPU KV-read baseline at equal peak HBM bandwidth (A100-B200), for 32K-token contexts across evaluated 30B-175B MHA models, approaching the 2x upper bound from halving historical memory traffic.

items.title: GlyphAtlas: Disentangling Stroke Detail from Layout for Scene Text Synthesis
items.summary: Scene text synthesis requires stroke-accurate characters rendered in a specified layout, as well as visual coherence with the surrounding scene. To achieve this, existing methods commonly pre-render the target text at its intended locations to form a glyph image that jointly specifies layout and glyph structure. However, this representation ties the resolution of each glyph to its target region, limiting fine-grained stroke guidance for small, densely packed, or structurally complex text. To tackle this, we propose GlyphAtlas, a scene text synthesis framework that retains the glyph image as a spatial anchor and supplies fine-grained stroke references through a dedicated glyph atlas. The atlas renders and encodes each character or word in a separate cell, decoupling reference resolution from target-region size. We further introduce atlas-anchored attention, which lets each text region retrieve stroke detail only from its corresponding atlas cells to refine the coarse glyph structure provided by the glyph image. This coarse-to-fine conditioning simplifies stroke rendering while preserving explicit layout correspondence. We optimize GlyphAtlas with a mask-weighted flow matching objective and a timestep-weighted text perceptual loss for writing accuracy and background consistency. Random resolution augmentation of atlas cells supports adjustable atlas budgets at inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GlyphAtlas achieves stroke-accurate synthesis of small, dense, and structurally complex text, zero-shot transfer to languages unseen during task-specific training, and leading performance in scenes with many text regions. project page: https://fr0zencrane.github.io/project-glyphatlas/

items.title: DT-MATCH: Defect- and Topology-Aware Chiplet Matching for Yield Optimization in Heterogeneous Integration
items.summary: Heterogeneous integration (HI) and advanced packaging enable chiplet-based system-on-chip (SoC) designs; however, they also introduce new yield challenges arising from manufacturing defects and complex die-to-die (D2D) interconnect constraints. In particular, lane-level defects, limited spares, and strict structural compatibility requirements impede the efficient assembly of functional systems from defective but repairable chiplets. We present DT-MATCH, a defect- and topology-aware chiplet matching framework that maximizes the number of functional SoCs under realistic assembly constraints. DT-MATCH provides two complementary approaches. The integer linear programming (ILP)-based approach is implemented using a batching strategy to approximate the exact formulation. The greedy randomized adaptive search procedure (GRASP)-based approach provides substantial acceleration, but it does not guarantee yield optimality. Both approaches use a preprocessing pipeline to reduce the problem size. Experimental results on industrial designs demonstrate that, as expected, the ILP-based approach achieves superior solution quality. The GRASP-based approach leads to lower runtimes while still achieving solution quality that is comparable to the ILP-based solution. Together, these methods provide a trade-off between solution quality and efficiency for practical chiplet assembly optimization.

items.title: Mutable Inference: Architecting LLM Accelerators for Inference-Time Learning
items.summary: Long-context LLMs must retain growing histories, but full attention makes each new token increasingly expensive. Inference-time learning (ITL) offers another approach. The model keeps training on the context during inference, retaining what it learns in its weights. Recent work shows that ITL can match full-context attention quality while attending only to a recent fixed-size window. This bounds attention costs but adds Learning (backward computation and weight updates) alongside Prediction (the forward pass) costs. Inference accelerators assume fixed weights, while training accelerators target complete training steps. This work identifies two opportunities. Attention's non-matrix operations leave enough idle matrix capacity for Learning, while selected layers can tolerate delayed weight updates with little quality loss. We exploit both with Learning While Serving (LWS), an inference accelerator architecture that shares compute hardware between latency-critical Prediction and deadline-flexible Learning. Hardware-managed per-layer weight versioning allows Learning to publish updates while in-flight computations read older versions. Resumable reduction blocks let Learning kernels span fragmented idle windows and yield to Prediction, while dedicated softmax-gradient units relieve vector contention. On modeled datacenter and edge NPUs, LWS hides Learning within Prediction, sustaining Prediction-only throughput while preserving 99.3% of fully fresh Learning's quality benefit for TTT-E2E 3B at 128K tokens. Across nine models, LWS achieves 1.6x the throughput of serial execution and 1.3x that of the best prior co-execution architecture. RTL synthesis shows that LWS adds 1.5% to NPU core area without another MAC array. By efficiently turning idle inference capacity into learning capacity, LWS establishes inference-time learning as a first-class workload for future LLM accelerators.

items.title: The Transformer Paradigm: Dynamic Processing and a New Principle of Inference
items.summary: We argue that the Transformer revolution is not adequately understood as a merely quantitative expansion of deep learning, but as the emergence of a new paradigm based on a different principle of inference. We interpret the Transformer as a system in which token representations are transformed by parameterized transformations, or transforming concepts. During inference, some of these transformations are dynamically constructed from the current input: previously acquired transformations are first adapted and then applied. At the mechanical-structural level, this dynamic processing is realized through output-weight interconnections, whereby outputs of some networks determine the weights of others. The resulting mode of processing, which we call Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (SIDPP), provides a framework for explaining strong prompt sensitivity and opens research directions concerning interpretability, control, alternative AI architectures, neuromorphic systems, and possible biological realizations of dynamic processing.

items.title: TIDE: Reclaiming Lost Performance In On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Synchronous, colocated RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) today suffers from severe under-utilization due to long-tail rollouts. Inference engines fall idle waiting for long-tail rollouts or decode at low, inefficient batch sizes. To address this, we present TIDE, an RL training system that preserves on-policy training semantics while recovering resource utilization. TIDE does so by two complementary techniques: (1) dynamically repurposing rollout GPUs for training while long-tail rollouts complete and (2) dynamically migrating rollouts between inference engines to boost decoding throughput. TIDE automatically determines the right time to repurpose rollout resources through an adaptive migration policy, obtaining performance improvements that generalize across multiple applications and hardware configurations without requiring bespoke configuration. In our evaluation, TIDE provides end-to-end speedups of up to 1.36x over colocated systems, outperforming all evaluated on-policy baselines and achieving up to 97% of optimal throughput.

items.title: Providing Accuracy Guarantees for the Fixed-Point Emulation of Matrix Multiplication
items.summary: Fixed-point methods such as Ozaki-II emulate double-precision matrix multiplication (GEMM) on fast low-precision hardware. Software that chooses the mantissa bit count automatically is numerically safe when the emulated product keeps the error guarantee of the floating-point GEMM it replaces. We analyze the worst-case and average-case error of fixed-point and floating-point dot products, define exponent span capacities that determine the extra mantissa bits an input requires, and approximate them with a low-precision GEMM. We prove that 53 bits plus such a capacity and a small constant preserve the classical worst-case error bound for a floating-point dot product, and we demonstrate this guarantee in software on several test cases. In a developer build of cuBLAS on an NVIDIA B200, each implemented bit-count rule earns grade~A on Test~2c of ``Grading the BLAS'' at every size and exponent range tested, falling back to double precision at the widest ranges; in exact arithmetic, the bound holds on every adversarial and random input tested.

items.title: CoSyDelay: Cognitive Symbolic Regression for Traffic Delay Estimation
items.summary: Trustworthy estimation of traffic delays at signalized intersections is critical for modern transportation systems, as it supports proactive traffic control for congestion mitigation. Existing analytical methods often rely on idealized assumptions that limit their accuracy under complex traffic conditions, whereas data-driven methods may achieve strong estimation performance but usually lack transparent structures, which reduces confidence in their practical application. To address these limitations, we propose CoSyDelay, a cognitive symbolic regression (SR) framework for automatically deriving explicit and physically consistent empirical delay estimation expressions (DEEs). Specifically, CoSyDelay decomposes intersection-level delay estimation into turning-movement-level subproblems, thereby reducing the complexity of the symbolic search. During DEE learning, CoSyDelay constructs domain-informed symbolic inputs from traffic variables. Large language models (LLMs) are employed as symbolic search operators to iteratively generate and refine candidate expression structures, whose movement-specific coefficients are subsequently calibrated using approach-level delay labels. A composite fitness function evaluates the learned DEEs jointly in terms of estimation accuracy and compliance with specified traffic-delay principles. Experimental results on multiple signalized intersections demonstrate that the resulting expressions achieve competitive estimation performance while maintaining physical consistency, thereby supporting trustworthy delay estimation. Source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ForrestXie9/CoSyDelay.

items.summary: Learning manipulation tasks from few demonstrations requires abstractions that capture the changes relevant to task completion, such as object poses in rigid-body manipulation. items.title: A predictive, per-engine energy roofline of the Apple Neural Engine
items.summary: The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) is in over a billion devices, but is characterized indirectly via CoreML. Using a CoreML-free fused-graph dispatch path, we measure the ANE, along with the Apple GPU and CPU on the same device, with per-engine energy accounting. The consumer-available roofline does not predict the ANE in practice. A critical correction is that the ANE sees two effective memory bandwidths: a slow activation path and a fast weight-stream path. Two roofline ridges follow, and the weight-stream ridge is below that of the GPU. The ANE single-operand compute peak decreases instead of plateauing. Its weight stream is byte-bound in fp16 but limited by the dequantizer's element rate in int8. As a result, int8 compression saves energy at unchanged throughput and an int4 lookup-table stream raises throughput and efficiency at a cost of 2.55 points of ImageNet top-1. The corrected roofline identifies the lower-energy ANE paths and bounds it from below. A constructed device map reproduces across four unique ANE generations. Results show that operators should be placed by arithmetic intensity and fused for optimal performance.

items.title: PerfArena: Ranking LLMs by Code Performance
items.summary: Industry now relies on LLMs to write a large share of production code. Although that code is mostly, but not always, correct, correctness alone does not determine whether it is fit for repeated and extensive use, which depends on what the code costs in time, memory and energy. Most code-generation benchmarks nonetheless evaluate correctness in isolation, and most performance-oriented benchmarks cover few languages and rarely measure energy consumption. To address this gap, we present PERFARENA, an open-source, reproducible arena that ranks LLMs by the performance of their generated code across multiple languages and competitions. PERFARENA executes the solutions of each LLM on a Unix-like host and reports correctness together with latency, peak memory, and energy consumption. Correctness oracles, performance oracles, profilers, and code-generation workflows are pluggable in PERFARENA, enabling the integration of new judging backends and measurement tools without changing the pipeline. We evaluate PERFARENA on two competitions: CLBGComp, 10 compute-intensive benchmarks from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game, and LeetCodeComp, 99 LeetCode problems whose accepted solutions differ measurably in latency. Currently, PERFARENA holds 9,455 correct and measured solutions from 13 state-of-the-art LLMs across 7 programming languages. Across both competitions, got-6-astra is the only LLM that no other LLM beats significantly in latency, energy consumption, or peak memory, solving 99.7% of LeetCodeComp and 100% of CLBGComp. All PERFARENA leaderboards and measured solutions are publicly available, providing a continuously updated reference that helps developers choose an LLM per language and metric, instead of relying only on correctness rates or pricing.

items.title: Streaming across viewing conditions - The effect of viewing distance and display luminance on video quality
items.summary: The visibility of streamed video distortions is affected by the user's display and viewing conditions, such as their display's luminance or the viewing distance. Distortions become less visible at lower luminance levels or farther viewing distances. However, most image and video quality metrics assume fixed optimal display and viewing conditions, making them insensitive to the viewing conditions. In this work, we demonstrate how existing metrics can be adapted to account for both factors and compare such an adaptation with the metrics that natively model viewing conditions. First, we collected a new video quality dataset, HDR-VDC, which contains streaming distortions in 4K HDR videos. The dataset consists of 12 4K and 4 FHD HDR source video content, each distorted with AV1 encoding and Lanczos upscaling from a lower resolution. The quality loss due to the distortions was measured at two viewing distances, corresponding to 60 and 120 pixels per visual degree, and two display mean luminance levels, varying by a factor of 8 in terms of luminance. Next, we developed a pre-processing framework that lets us adapt many quality metrics so that they can evaluate content across the viewing distances and luminance levels. The framework employs a display model and perceptually uniform encoding, PU21, to account for the effect of display luminance, and perspective projection scaling (PPS) to account for the effect of viewing distance. We used the framework to compare the performance of 35 state-of-the-art metrics. This allowed us to identify a selection of existing quality metrics that can be effectively adapted to account for the viewing conditions.

items.title: A Matrix with Steps: An Episodic and Procedural Memory Method for Tool-Using Agents and Robots
items.summary: Agents that call tools and robots that execute tasks are challenged by two shortcomings: they repeat what failed before, and they learn from runs that they only believe succeeded. We describe the construction of a memory that addresses both, built for a production agent platform. Every run is recorded as an episode, and only an outcome confirmed by an external check, a test, a tool result or a person counts; the agent's own claim never does. What is learned from episodes is kept in a memory with two parts: an associative matrix, written with the delta rule, which finds the procedure that applies to a situation; and a section of ordered, addressable step records that answers what comes after a given step, where a step is a goal of the agent, not a motion. Because the matrix sums its associations, it keeps no order and cannot return or delete a single one; it serves as the finder, and order, outcome counts and deletion live in the records. We describe how execution outcomes are stored, how episodes are recalled and used for solving tasks, and the file format that stores the memory. In simulation, a robot that judged its own success and stopped when it believed it was done reported $96\%$ of its tasks as done and solved $35\%$; with external verification it solved $79%$. In a store of $100000$ synthetic episodes ($457$MB on disk), the oldest episode was still found first, no episode from another person's memory was returned, and a success vouched for only by the model was never recalled; a lookup took $16$ms on a laptop and $40$ms on a server node (median). Task outcomes were measured up to about $10000$ confirmed records, where the exact records solved every revisit at the first attempt.

items.title: Glance, then Select: Evidence-Tempered Visual Token Selection for Extremely Compressed Multimodal LLMs
items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) encode a high-resolution image into thousands of visual tokens, which dominate the cost of the prefill stage. Visual token reduction removes most of these tokens, but two problems remain at extreme budgets. The vision encoder still processes every patch of the image, and the few surviving tokens often miss the small regions that hold the answer. In this paper, we propose Glance-ETD, a two-stage token reduction framework guided by a lightweight question-conditioned scorer. In the first stage, a glance encoder views the image at low resolution and re-encodes only the question-relevant regions at native resolution. In the second stage, Evidence-Tempered Diversity (ETD) selects the final tokens by combining diversity with the evidence predicted by the scorer, so that the kept tokens cover the scene and retain the answer. A single-rollout self-distillation recipe trains the MLLM with the glance encoder. With only 5% of the visual tokens, Glance-ETD retains 91.6% of the full-token performance of Qwen3.5-4B across fourteen benchmarks and outperforms the strongest prior method, LT-OPD, by 17.3 points and the same training recipe with DivPrune by 6.0. It also speeds up the time to first token on 4K images by 3.1x and generalizes to three other MLLMs and to high-resolution document benchmarks, with the largest gains on text-rich tasks.

items.title: This robot helps you lift objects — by looking at your biceps
items.summary: This robot helps you lift objects — by looking at your biceps rachelg Wed, 05/22/2019 - 10:30 Video May 22 '19 Rachel Gordon CSAIL system can mirror a user's motions and follow nonverbal commands by monitoring arm muscles. We humans are very good at collaboration. For instance, when two people work together to carry a heavy object like a table or a sofa, they tend to instinctively coordinate their motions, constantly recalibrating to make sure their hands are at the same height as the other person's. Our natural ability to make these types of adjustments allows us to collaborate on tasks big and small. But a computer or a robot still can't follow a human's lead with ease. We usually either explicitly program them using machine-speak, or train them to understand our words, à la virtual assistants like Siri or Alexa. In contrast, researchers at MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) recently showed that a smoother robot-human collaboration is possible through a new system they developed, where machines help people lift objects by monitoring their muscle movements. Dubbed RoboRaise, the system involves putting electromyography (EMG) sensors on a user's biceps and triceps to monitor muscle activity. Its algorithms then continuously detect changes to the person's arm level, as well as discrete up-and-down hand gestures the user might make for finer motor control. The team used the system for a series of tasks involving picking up and assembling mock airplane components. In experiments, users worked on these tasks with the robot and were able to control it to within a few inches of the desired heights by lifting and then tensing their arm. It was more accurate when gestures were used, and the robot responded correctly to roughly 70 percent of all gestures. Graduate student Joseph DelPreto says he could imagine people using RoboRaise to help in manufacturing and construction settings, or even as an assistant around the house. "Our approach to lifting objects with a robot aims to be intuitive and similar to how you might lift something with another person — roughly copying each other's motions while inferring helpful adjustments," says DelPreto, lead author on a new paper about the project with MIT Professor and CSAIL Director Daniela Rus. "The key insight is to use nonverbal cues that encode instructions for how to coordinate, for example to lift a little higher or lower. Using muscle signals to communicate almost makes the robot an extension of yourself that you can fluidly control." The project builds off the team's existing system that allows users to instantly correct robot mistakes with brainwaves and hand gestures, now enabling continuous motion in a more collaborative way. "We aim to develop human-robot interaction where the robot adapts to the human, rather than the other way around. This way the robot becomes an intelligent tool for physical work," says Rus. EMG signals can be tricky to work with: They're often very noisy, and it can be difficult to predict exactly how a limb is moving based on muscle activity. Even if you can estimate how a person is moving, how you want the robot itself to respond may be unclear. RoboRaise gets around this by putting the human in control. The team's system uses noninvasive, on-body sensors that detect the firing of neurons as you tense or relax muscles. Using wearables also gets around problems of occlusions or ambient noise, which can complicate tasks involving vision or speech. RoboRaise's algorithm then processes biceps activity to estimate how the person's arm is moving so the robot can roughly mimic it, and the person can slightly tense or relax their arm to move the robot up or down. If a user needs the robot to move farther away from their own position or hold a pose for a while, they can just gesture up or down for finer control; a neural network detects these gestures at any time based on biceps and triceps activity. A new user can start using the system very quickly, with minimal calibration. After putting on the sensors, they just need to tense and relax their arm a few times then lift a light weight to a few heights. The neural network that detects gestures is only trained on data from previous users. The team tested the system with 10 users through a series of three lifting experiments: one where the robot didn't move at all, another where the robot moved in response to their muscles but didn't help lift the object, and a third where the robot and person lifted an object together. When the person had feedback from the robot — when they could see it moving or when they were lifting something together — the achieved height was significantly more accurate compared to having no feedback. The team also tested RoboRaise on assembly tasks, such as lifting a rubber sheet onto a base structure. It was able to successfully lift both rigid and flexible objects onto the bases. RoboRaise was implemented on the team's Baxter humanoid robot, but the team says it could be adapted for any robotic platform. In the future, the team hopes that adding more muscles or different types of sensors to the system will increase the degrees of freedom, with the ultimate goal of doing even more complex tasks. Cues like exertion or fatigue from muscle activity could also help robots provide more intuitive assistance. The team tested one version of the system that uses biceps and triceps levels to tell the robot how stiffly the person is holding their end of the object; together, the human and machine could fluidly drag an object around or rigidly pull it taut. The team will present their work at the International Conference on Robotics and Automation this week in Montreal, Canada. The project was funded in part by The Boeing Company. items.title: Evidence-Governed Adoption of Self-Generated Updates in Autonomous AI Agents
items.summary: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits, requires meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. We establish an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent calibration samples comparing the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference procedure. We also formalise reference replacement through bridge tests, derive a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage, and provide an audit-planning condition relating effect-size margin, sample sizes, and acceptance probability. A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The guarantees are conditional on bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference-evaluation construct, and declared evaluation distributions; they do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.

items.title: Predicting, Fast and Slow: SSD Already Knows Which Guess Is Wrong
items.summary: Heimdall, a learned controller, calls slow on 52% of an SSD's reads when 30% are slow. Uncertainty estimators, the remedy prescribed for its wrong guesses, cannot find them: nine of them do no better than a coin. The drive can. On one trace, 2% of the reads of 4 to 8 KiB that found less than 4 KiB outstanding while the drive was answering came back slow, and Heimdall called 96% of them slow. A 4,096-entry table of how the drive's recent reads came back, untrained and 21 ns a decision, ranks the wrong guesses at a median AUROC of 0.68 on 57 held-out traces, where the nine sit at 0.46 to 0.52, and it predicts slow reads better than Heimdall itself.

items.title: Coordinating Distributed AI Servers with Industrial Loads to Reduce Grid-Interconnection Needs
items.summary: We show that co-locating distributed AI servers with industrial demand and coordinating AI workloads with production loads can substantially reduce the additional grid interconnection that AI computing requires. Grid interconnection is increasingly constraining the expansion of large AI data centers. Factories already have grid connections sized for their peak production loads, and we propose hosting AI servers during production valleys. We formulate a joint optimization that sizes CPU and GPU servers, schedules deadline-constrained tasks, and routes tasks among factories, and use it to compare three factory-site architectures with new large data centers serving the same demand. Applying this framework to 31 Chinese manufacturing industries, we find that AI demand and production loads often do not peak together. As a result, AI servers placed at factories and scheduled according to production peaks need about 60% less additional interconnection capacity than new large data centers, and 98% less when tasks are routed among a group's factories.

items.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
items.summary: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.
